hints: Count carefully using the key. How many solid long polypeptides and how many dashed short polypeptides make up this one molecule?
Remember what each level means: alpha-helix is secondary, folding of one chain is tertiary, but joining of two or more separate polypeptides together is quaternary.
walkthrough:
**Count the polypeptides in the molecule**

Look at the key and the diagram. There are 2 long polypeptides (solid lines) twisted into the fibre and heads.

Then add the short ones: 2 short polypeptides (dashed lines) bind to each head, so 2 x 2 = 4 short polypeptides. Total = 2 + 4 = 6 polypeptides in one molecule.

**Recall the four levels of protein structure**

Secondary structure is local coiling into an alpha-helix or folding into a beta-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds.

Tertiary structure is the further 3D folding of a single polypeptide into a globular shape. Quaternary structure is the assembly of two or more separate polypeptide chains into one functional protein.

**Match the molecule to the correct level**

Although this molecule *contains* alpha-helices and globular heads, the whole molecule is made of six separate chains joined together.

Any protein with more than one polypeptide has quaternary structure, so A is the best description.

options.A: Correct. The functional molecule is an assembly of six separate polypeptides (2 long + 4 short), which is the definition of quaternary structure.
options.B: False. Alpha-helices are secondary structure, but the question asks about the structure of the whole six-chain molecule, not just that local feature.
options.C: False. Twisting of two separate chains together is not tertiary. Tertiary refers to folding within a single polypeptide only.
options.D: False. A globular shape alone does not make it tertiary when multiple separate polypeptides are joined. With several chains, it is quaternary.
